idiom_name: goroutine per subtask + channel/WaitGroup join (runtime work-stealing scheduler)
implementation_notes: Go has no task class and no fork/join pool API: the idiom is to fork with `go` and join with a channel receive, sync.WaitGroup (WaitGroup.Go/Wait, Add/Done) or an errgroup.Group. Recursion stays ordinary Go - the decomposition is just a function calling itself. The runtime supplies the pool and the stealing: goroutines run on per-P run queues, and idle Ps pick up (steal) runnable goroutines, so nothing is written to balance work. Build a worker pool by hand only when you need bounded concurrency with backpressure or a lower task rate; the classic RecursiveTask-style task structure is never worth emulating.
code_sketch:
func sum(a []int) int64 {
    if len(a) < 1_000 { return seqSum(a) }        // leaf
    mid := len(a) / 2
    ch := make(chan int64, 2)                     // fork
    go func() { ch <- sum(a[:mid]) }()
    go func() { ch <- sum(a[mid:]) }()
    return <-ch + <-ch                            // join
}
pitfalls: Every fork needs a completing join: an unbalanced path that never receives leaks goroutines - use errgroup/context so a failing subtree can stop the rest.
Recursion multiplies goroutines per level: cheap compared to threads, but a missing threshold still floods the scheduler and the garbage collector.
For non-recursive fan-out prefer sync.WaitGroup (or WaitGroup.Go) over one channel per task; channels cost an allocation and a scheduler handoff, and a closed-channel send panics.
